captions.text: That's right. It directs federal agencies to update their maps, documents and databases with the new name.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Has he done something like this before?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, on his first day back in office he renamed the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Why do this now, with Lake Ontario?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It comes amid his trade war with Canada. He even signed the order in front of a Great Lakes map with 'Lake America' printed over it.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Is there something behind the trade dispute itself?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: He's claimed farmers face a 400% tariff, though most US agricultural exports to Canada actually enter duty-free. Some items, like over-quota eggs and dairy, do face steep Canadian tariffs.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So the name change is really tied to that bigger dispute.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It seems to be part of the same moment, yes.

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 木曜日、トランプ氏がオンタリオ湖の名称を変更する大統領令に署名しました。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 新しい名前は『レイク・アメリカ』です。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 連邦機関には、地図や文書、データベースでこの名称を使うよう求めています。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 背景にはカナダとの貿易摩擦の激化があります。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 就任初日にメキシコ湾を『アメリカ湾』に改称した動きと同じ流れです。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 会見場には五大湖の地図が置かれ、赤字で新名称が記されていました。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: トランプ氏は米国の農家が400%の関税を課されていると述べました。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 実際には対カナダ農産品輸出の約97%が無関税で取引されています。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 割当を超えた卵や乳製品にだけ、カナダ側で最大300%の関税がかかります。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 地名ひとつにも、政治のいまが映し出されているようです。

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So El Niño isn't just a natural cycle anymore?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It's still natural, but this study finds it's being supercharged by fossil fuel warming.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Supercharged how, exactly?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: The strong El Niño events of recent decades appear stronger because of the planet's overall overheating.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Is there one happening right now?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, researchers describe a major one currently brewing, set to affect weather worldwide.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Why does this finding matter so much to scientists?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It helps answer a long-unclear question: whether climate change is actually changing how strong El Niño gets.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: And who ends up dealing with the fallout?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Countries already facing heatwaves, wildfires, and flooding — often people who've contributed least to causing this.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So next year could be especially hot.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: That's the expectation — El Niño combined with this warming trend makes it almost certain to be a record year.

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 今、太平洋で強いエルニーニョが育っていて、「ゴジラ級」と呼ばれています。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: この現象は世界中の天候を大きく揺さぶるとみられています。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 新しい研究によると、その勢いは化石燃料による地球温暖化で強められているそうです。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: これまで気候変動がエルニーニョの強さに影響しているかは、はっきり分かっていませんでした。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 今回の研究が、その長年の疑問に一つの答えを示しました。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: すでに熱波や山火事、洪水に苦しむ国々にとって、これは重い意味を持ちます。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 特に、温暖化の原因をほとんど作っていない人たちほど、大きな打撃を受けるといいます。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: エルニーニョは元々、世界の気温を押し上げる働きがあります。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 来年は観測史上最も暑い年になる可能性がほぼ確実だそうです。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 朝の空気は変わらなくても、地球の裏側では大きな変化が進んでいます。

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So three UK airports were hit by a cyber-attack?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, Manchester, London Stansted, and East Midlands. Data from about 8.7 million customers was accessed.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: That's a lot of people. Were any flights affected?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: No, the company said operations weren't disrupted, and passenger safety or aviation security wasn't compromised.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So it was really about data, not the airports themselves.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Right. And this happened during the busy summer travel season, when a lot of people are flying.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: What's the company doing about it now?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: A MAG spokesperson said they immediately contained the risk and are working with specialist advisers to protect customers and systems.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Did they tell customers anything directly?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, London Stansted emailed customers urging caution around unexpected emails, calls, or texts claiming to be from them.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So the real risk now is people getting targeted afterward.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Exactly, that's why they're asking everyone to stay alert.

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: イギリスのマンチェスター、ロンドン・スタンステッド、イーストミッドランズの3空港がサイバー攻撃を受けました。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 約870万人分の顧客データが不正に閲覧されたということです。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 運営会社は、乗客の安全や航空保安には影響がなかったと説明しています。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 空港の運営自体も通常どおり続けられていました。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 攻撃が起きたのは、夏の旅行シーズンの真っ只中でした。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 利用者の多い時期だったため、影響を受けた人の数も大きくなっています。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 運営会社のMAGは、リスクを直ちに抑え込んだとしています。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 専門家の助言を受けながら、顧客とシステムの保護を進めているそうです。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: スタンステッド空港は利用者に対し、空港を名乗る不審な連絡に注意するよう呼びかけました。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 心当たりのないメールや電話には、いつも以上に注意を払っておきたいところです。

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So Meta is paying $18 billion? That sounds huge.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It is a big number, but it's spread over a decade, and Meta denies any wrongdoing.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: What was the settlement actually about?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It resolves claims from 52 US attorneys general that Meta designed products to be addictive to children and misled people about their safety.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: If they deny wrongdoing, why settle at all?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Because Meta made around $60bn in profit last year, so this payment is fairly small for them financially.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Didn't they try fighting this kind of case before?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, just months ago Meta fought a similar case in court and lost significantly.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So settling now looks like a smarter move?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It seems that way. The economics of fighting these cases have clearly shifted for Meta.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So this settlement is really just one part of a longer story.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Exactly. It's manageable now, but the broader pressure on Meta isn't going away.

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: Metaが52の米州司法長官との間で、180億ドルの支払いに合意したという話です。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 子どもたちを依存させる設計をし、安全性について誤解を与えていたという訴えに関するものです。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: Meta側はいまも不正行為を否定していますが、支払いは十年ほどに分けて行うとされています。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: この金額だけを見れば大きく感じますが、Metaは昨年およそ600億ドルの利益を上げています。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: つまり同社にとっては、痛みというより整理費用のような規模だと言えます。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 興味深いのは、わずか数か月前まで法廷で争う姿勢を見せていたことです。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: その裁判では大きく敗れていて、今回の和解はそこからの方針転換にも見えます。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 訴訟を続けるより、早めに手を打つ方が得策だという判断が働いたのでしょう。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: こうした計算は、これから他の企業にも広がっていくかもしれません。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 静かな朝ですが、テクノロジー企業を取り巻く空気は少しずつ変わりつつあります。

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So what's happening Thursday night?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: A near total lunar eclipse, visible across North and South America.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Near total? How close does it get?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: At its peak, 96% of the moon will be darkened by Earth's shadow.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Why does that happen exactly?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Earth moves between the sun and moon, casting its shadow onto the lunar surface.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: I've heard people call these 'blood moons.' Why is that?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: The shadow appears reddish, because of how sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Is this connected to that solar eclipse people saw over Europe?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Different event, but related. That one saw the moon block the sun, bringing daytime darkness to parts of the continent.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Sounds like a good week for skywatchers.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It is. Millions are expected to see this one.

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 木曜の夜、南北アメリカの空に大きな天体ショーが訪れます。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 月のおよそ九十六パーセントが地球の影に隠れる、ほぼ皆既に近い月食です。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 大気中で屈折した太陽光の影響で、影が赤く染まるため「ブラッドムーン」と呼ばれます。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 好条件のため、肉眼でも十分に楽しめる見込みです。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 地球が太陽の光を遮る位置に来ると、その影が月面に届きます。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: これが月食という現象の仕組みです。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 今月初めには欧州で、逆に太陽が月に隠れる皆既日食が起きました。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: あの時は昼間なのに、一部地域が暗闇に包まれました。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 短い間に、月と太陽それぞれの姿が変わる瞬間を人々は目にしたことになります。

captions.speaker: narrator
captions.text: 空を見上げるだけで、宇宙の動きを身近に感じられる夜です。

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: What's the latest on that flood in Nepal?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: At least 90 Americans are still missing, part of nearly 2,000 unaccounted for after the flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Why were so many Americans out there?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Many were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a site sacred to several faiths, including Hinduism and Buddhism.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Was it a large group traveling together?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes. Twenty-two Americans returning from a pilgrimage hosted by the Isha Foundation were among 80 foundation members not yet located.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Has anyone spoken about them personally?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: One person, Crespi, described the trekkers as 'like family,' saying it had been a lifelong dream for many to make that trip.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: How serious has this become overall?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: The official death toll is nearing 600 and expected to keep rising, with survivors, victims, and missing people from many nationalities.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: It's hard to imagine what families are going through right now.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It is. Search efforts continue as officials try to account for everyone still unreported.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So the President just created a Space Academy?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, he signed an executive order establishing it — the country's first.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: When did this happen?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Friday, at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Texas, during an event honoring the Artemis II crew.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Did he explain what it's for?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: He told the astronauts and NASA staff there, 'It's called the US Space Academy.'

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Is it modeled on something existing?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: He compared it to institutions like the Naval Academy and West Point.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So it's meant to be a serious training institution, not just symbolic.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: That seems to be the idea, given those comparisons.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Why does this matter right now?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Because space has remained a major priority throughout both of Trump's terms.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So actors are campaigning against AI voice cloning now?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, Nicola Coughlan, Hugh Bonneville and Matt Lucas are among those backing it.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: What's their main worry?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Bonneville put it simply — he said his voice is unique, it's his, part of his identity.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Is this just about actors protecting their work?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Not only that. The campaign says 28% of UK adults report being targeted by a voice-cloning scam.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: That's a lot of ordinary people affected.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It is. About 80 people signed an open letter to the prime minister and Andy Burnham over it.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So what are they actually asking for?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: There's a Gov.uk petition asking for everyone in Britain to legally own their own voice, as part of their statutory rights.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Makes sense — your voice really is personal.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: That's the heart of it. As Bonneville said, it's one of his tools, and it's his.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So there's a new rule about how datacentres get their power?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, national laws are being drawn up, and Chris Bowen says there won't be any special exceptions for Queensland or the Northern Territory.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Those two states wanted to use coal and gas for their datacentres, right?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: That's right. The Northern Territory's Finocchiaro pointed to gas from the Beetaloo basin project as an option, and Queensland's Crisafulli argued his state can control its own energy mix because the system there is state-owned.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: And Bowen's response to that was?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: He called it 'a very hard thing to do' — meaning those states will still need to make their case to the national regulator, not just assume an exemption.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: What was Albanese's take after the meeting in Sydney?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: He described the outcome as allowing some flexibility for governments that own their power systems, without abandoning the broader push.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Why does this actually matter for people at home?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Albanese went in wanting new rules that favour renewable energy and stop datacentres from driving up power prices for households and businesses.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: And this will all be debated in parliament?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, that's expected to happen next year.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So West Point fired its only climate scientist? What happened exactly?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: A lawsuit says he was let go after refusing an order to stop teaching about the human causes of climate change.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Refusing an order — that sounds tense. Was there a specific moment?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, the lawsuit describes him telling a superior, Kalkstein, that Trump was commander in chief and sets the agenda, then leaving the meeting.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Is this the only case like this at West Point?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: No, it's actually the second lawsuit over academic freedom concerns filed by an educator there.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: What does his lawyer say about why he pushed back?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: His attorney, Michael Sussman, says he's a conservative Republican who believes cadets need the facts on climate change for national security reasons.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Was there anything happening at West Point around the same time that might connect to this?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: He reportedly learned his job was at risk in May, when the academy announced cuts to civilian staff while also opening a new humanities center needing geography teachers.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So the details are still playing out through the courts.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: That's right — this is now part of the ongoing legal record.
